resources.string: Daily Stoic quote and reflection reminder
What will you make of the weeks that remain?
“Think of yourself as dead. You have lived your life. Now take what’s left and live it properly.”
Memento mori is not pessimism. It is clarity. When we remember time is finite, trivial worries lose power and the essential becomes visible: character, attention, and action in the present day.
“You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.”
“It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.”
“No man has power over the future. The present alone is ours.”

Use the weeks grid as a daily orientation tool: not to create fear, but to increase intention. Each filled week is evidence that life is moving. Ask one concrete question each morning: What matters enough to deserve this day?
“If this week were all you had, what would be the most Stoic use of it?”
Some things are in our control and others not.
What is weighing on your mind?
Is this something you can act on, or must you let it go?
Take action on these. Mark done when complete.
Write down something that is worrying or stressing you.
Ask: is this within my control? Sort it honestly.
If yes — define one action and take it. If no — release it and move on.
What specific action will you take?
A daily practice rooted in two thousand years of Stoic philosophy.
A new Stoic quote awaits you each morning at 7:00 AM. You can change this time in Settings.

Ataraxy is a tool for personal reflection and Stoic philosophy exploration. It is not a substitute for professional mental health treatment, therapy, or medical advice. If you are experiencing mental health challenges, please seek help from a qualified healthcare professional.

Ataraxy is a personal reflection tool designed to help you explore Stoic philosophy through daily quotes, guided practices, and journaling. The goal is to cultivate tranquility and resilience through the wisdom of Stoic philosophers.

This app is grounded in ancient Stoic philosophy, which teaches that we cannot control external events, but we can control our responses to them. Through reflection, journaling, and practicing Stoic principles, we can develop emotional resilience and mental tranquility.

Much of the content in this app — including author biographies, quote attributions, sub-concept descriptions, and practice prompts — was researched and drafted with the assistance of AI. While every effort has been made to ensure accuracy and faithfulness to the original sources, we encourage you to consult primary texts for scholarly or serious study.
Begin with intention. Your morning practice awaits.
Reflect before rest. Your evening practice awaits.
